name: Argument from incredulity
statement: The argument from incredulity runs from 'I cannot imagine how P could be true' to 'P is false', and the premise is a report about the arguer.
meaning: The move has two directions. An inability to imagine how a claim could be true is offered as reason to think it false, and an inability to imagine how it could be false as reason to think it true. Both are versions of the appeal to ignorance, entry 413, with the failed search carried out inside one person's head rather than in the world. That puts the weight of the inference on a condition the arguer seldom states. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy sets the condition out for the parent fallacy: reasoning from a failed search is proper reasoning only if the proof attempts were quite thorough, and if a discoverable proof would exist were the thing real. An imagination meets neither test well. It samples what one person can picture, and long causal chains are the thing people are worst at picturing, so the inference is weakest exactly where it is reached for.

origin.note: The label appears in chapter 2, 'Good Design', where Dawkins writes that Bishop Hugh Montefiore 'makes heavy use of what may be called the Argument from Personal Incredulity'. He does not claim to have coined it, and he writes that it is 'an extremely weak argument, as Darwin himself noted'. The index of the scanned 1986 edition read for this entry lists the term at page 38. Whether the phrase was in print before 1986 is not settled here. The three book-wide full-text searches that would settle it were all unavailable on 17 August 2026: HathiTrust returned 403, Open Library's search inside returned a search-engine error, and the Google Books API returned a daily quota error.

evidence: The record is textual, and it starts before the name. Darwin put the incredulity in his own mouth in the first edition of the Origin: to suppose that the eye could have been formed by natural selection 'seems, I freely confess, absurd in the highest possible degree'. He then answers it. Given gradations, heritable variation and usefulness at each step, the difficulty of believing it is one 'though insuperable by our imagination, can hardly be considered real', and the reader's 'reason ought to conquer his imagination'. Dawkins builds the modern case as a list. He collects a run of phrases from a single chapter of Montefiore, from 'there seems no explanation on Darwinian grounds' through 'I cannot see how' to 'It is difficult to see', and says most modern biologists would not find it difficult to explain every one of the Bishop's 35 examples, though not all are as easy as the polar bears. His handling of that one shows what the objection is: he translates the Bishop's puzzlement about white polar bears into a first-person sentence about a man sitting in his study, never having visited the Arctic, educated in classical literature and theology. Where measurement comes closest is in judgements of probability rather than of argument. Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 paper has a section headed 'Biases of imaginability'. Ten people can form 45 distinct committees of two and 45 of eight; the median estimate was 70 for committees of two and 20 for committees of eight. They write that the risk in an undertaking may be underestimated 'if some possible dangers are either difficult to conceive of, or simply do not come to mind'. Sherman, Cialdini, Schwartzman and Reynolds tested that in 1985 with a disease described as having easy-to-imagine or hard-to-imagine symptoms. Their abstract reports that subjects who found the symptoms hard to imagine judged the disease less likely, and that trying to imagine cognitively inaccessible events reduces likelihood estimates. Only the abstract was obtained and no figure from it is quoted.

replication.headline: No experiment on the inference itself was found. The nearest measured effects concern how likely something feels, not whether an argument from not being able to imagine it is any good.
replication.detail: The search was run again on 17 August 2026. It covered Crossref by bibliographic query on both names of the fallacy, PubMed on 'argument from incredulity' and on 'personal incredulity', and web search pairing the name with terms for experiment, participants and fallacy ratings. Crossref's matches under the name are Bebbington's two pages, Manninen's chapter and a blog post. PubMed returned 23 records and none of them is a test of the argument. OpenAlex could not be queried on that date, its API returning a daily quota error. Four reference works were read in full and none of them names this fallacy: Hansen's Stanford Encyclopedia entry on fallacies, the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's fallacy article, Hamblin's Fallacies of 1970 and Copi's Introduction to Logic of 1953. Martin Hinton's 2018 paper on arguments from ignorance in Informal Logic, also read in full, uses neither the word nor Dawkins' name. The measured neighbours have records of their own, and they are records of something else. The parent argument from ignorance is entry 413, which carries the Bayesian work on negative evidence. The illusion of explanatory depth is entry 110, and it runs the other way, being about people who believe they hold an explanation they cannot produce. Fernbach, Rogers, Fox and Sloman built the political version of that finding on Rozenblit and Keil's scale, writing that their instructions for rating understanding were modelled on it, and Crawford and Ruscio then failed to replicate the moderation they reported. Sloman and Vives write that the effect of explanation on people's sense of understanding 'has been replicated several times', while 'the effect on extremity is not so robust'. Entry 110 carries that dispute and its numbers. None of it tests an inference drawn from failing to imagine a mechanism.

limits: Walton's Arguments from Ignorance of 1996 is lending-restricted at the Internet Archive, its text could not be searched, and this page therefore says nothing about what is in it. Two other books that would show how logic's own literature handles this were obtained. Hamblin's Fallacies, the Methuen first edition of 1970, and Copi's Introduction to Logic, the Macmillan first edition of 1953, were read as full scanned text at the Internet Archive, and neither names the argument from incredulity. Both treat the argumentum ad ignorantiam. Copi files it among the fallacies of relevance and writes that it 'is fallacious in every context but one', the exception being a court of law, and Hamblin quotes that passage and objects that a form of argument valid now and invalid later, as presumptions change with context, is a strange one. Hansen's encyclopedia article cites Copi's 1961 edition rather than the 1953 one read here. What appears on this page about Walton is at one remove from Hansen, who places the appeal to ignorance among the argumentation schemes Walton classes as paralogisms. Two short treatments published under the fallacy's own name are paywalled and are named rather than used: Bebbington's two pages in Think, and Manninen's chapter in Bad Arguments. Both were closed at the publisher and at Unpaywall on 17 August 2026. Sherman and colleagues were read only through the abstract Crossref holds. That article was closed at Sage and recorded as closed by Unpaywall and OpenAlex on the same date, so this entry carries no sample size and no effect size for the one experiment closest to the topic. The Dawkins passages were read twice, once in the scanned text of the 1986 edition at the Internet Archive and once in the excerpt of chapter 2 posted on Dawkins' own newsletter, and the wording agrees.
misreadings: The name is Dawkins', the observation is not. Darwin stated the incredulity about the eye and answered it in 1859, and Dawkins says as much in the paragraph that names the argument. A second error reads him as dismissing appeals to improbability in general. He separates the serious versions from the naked ones, and writes that measuring the statistical improbability of a suggestion 'is the right way to go about assessing its believability'. His objection to C. E. Raven on cuckoos is that the sum was done wrong, not that sums are out of place. Third, the label is treated as a fixture of the fallacy literature when its home is popular scepticism. The Skeptic's Dictionary files it as the divine fallacy, in the form 'I can't figure this out, so a god must have done it'. The Wikipedia article, read on 17 August 2026, cites that dictionary, two websites and a critical-thinking textbook, and does not mention Dawkins at all. Fourth, the illusion of explanatory depth, entry 110, is not a measure of this argument. Rozenblit and Keil report that people feel they understand complex phenomena with greater precision, coherence and depth than they really do, which is confidence in an explanation somebody lacks rather than an inference drawn from lacking one.

sources.text: Dawkins, R. (1986). The Blind Watchmaker. Chapter 2, 'Good Design'. Read from the scanned text of the 1986 edition held in this Internet Archive item, as the file Dawkins,_Richard_-_The_Blind_Watchmaker_djvu.txt. Source for the naming passage, the list of Montefiore's phrases, the 35 examples, the polar bear translation and the index entry at page 38.

Dawkins, R. (2024). Good Design. The Poetry of Reality, 29 February 2024. An excerpt of chapter 2 of The Blind Watchmaker posted on Dawkins' own newsletter, fetched twice and used to confirm the wording taken from the scanned book.

Darwin, C. (1859). On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, first edition. Chapter VI, 'Organs of extreme perfection and complication'. Full text read at Project Gutenberg; source for the three quoted phrases about the eye and the imagination.

Hansen, H. Fallacies. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Read in full. Source for Locke's ad ignorantiam, for Copi's placement of it among informal fallacies of relevance, and for Walton's classification of it as a paralogism. The word 'incredulity' does not occur in the article.

Dowden, B. Fallacies. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Read in full. Source for the conditions under which an appeal to ignorance is proper reasoning. The word 'incredulity' does not occur in the article, which does list the appeal to ignorance and the availability heuristic.

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131. Full text read from a PDF of the article; the committee figures and the quoted sentence were extracted from the document text.

Sherman, S. J., Cialdini, R. B., Schwartzman, D. F., & Reynolds, K. D. (1985). Imagining Can Heighten or Lower the Perceived Likelihood of Contracting a Disease. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 11(1), 118-127. Described here from the abstract deposited at Crossref. Sage returned 403 on 17 August 2026, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex both recorded the article as closed with no repository copy on that date.

Rozenblit, L., & Keil, F. (2002). The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth. Cognitive Science, 26(5), 521-562. Full text read from the PDF posted on Keil's Yale cognitive development lab site, which is freely readable; the abstract sentence quoted here was read in that document. Entry 110 carries the study-by-study figures.

Fernbach, P. M., Rogers, T., Fox, C. R., & Sloman, S. A. (2013). Political Extremism Is Supported by an Illusion of Understanding. Psychological Science, 24(6), 939-946. Full text read from the repository copy hosted at ETH Zurich; source for the statement that its understanding-rating instructions were modelled on Rozenblit and Keil (2002).

Crawford, J. T., & Ruscio, J. (2021). Asking People to Explain Complex Policies Does Not Increase Political Moderation: Three Preregistered Failures to Closely Replicate Fernbach, Rogers, Fox, and Sloman's (2013) Findings. Psychological Science, 32(4), 611-621. Article not obtained, Unpaywall recording it as closed on 17 August 2026; the abstract at PubMed was read. Entry 110 carries its sample sizes.

Sloman, S. A., & Vives, M.-L. (2022). Is political extremism supported by an illusion of understanding? Cognition, 225, 105146. Full text read from a PDF; source for the two quoted judgements about which parts of the explanation effect have replicated.

Hinton, M. (2018). On arguments from ignorance. Informal Logic, 38(2), 184-212. Full text read from the journal's own PDF. Cited here for what it does not contain: the paper uses neither the word 'incredulity' nor Dawkins' name.

Hamblin, C. L. (1970). Fallacies. London: Methuen. Full scanned text read at the Internet Archive. Source for the objection to Copi's court-of-law exception, and cited for what it does not contain: the book does not name the argument from incredulity.

Copi, I. M. (1953). Introduction to Logic. New York: The Macmillan Company. Full scanned text of the first edition read at the Internet Archive. Source for the placement of the argumentum ad ignorantiam among the fallacies of relevance and for the quoted court-of-law exception. Hansen's encyclopedia article cites the 1961 edition, which was not read.

Bebbington, D. (2011). Argument from personal incredulity. Think, 10(28), 27-28. Paywalled and not obtained; the Crossref record and its short abstract were read on 17 August 2026, and Unpaywall recorded the article as closed. Named as one of the few pieces published under this heading.

Manninen, T. W. (2018). Appeal to Personal Incredulity. In Bad Arguments, 115-117. Wiley. Paywalled and not obtained; the Crossref record was read and Unpaywall recorded the chapter as closed on 17 August 2026. Named as a reference-work treatment under the fallacy's own name.

Walton, D. (1999). The Appeal to Ignorance, or Argumentum Ad Ignorantiam. Argumentation, 13(4), 367-377. Not obtained; the record was verified at Crossref and Unpaywall recorded it as closed on 17 August 2026, with the author's own paper archive at dougwalton.ca no longer serving files. Named as the standard treatment of the parent argument, and no claim on this page rests on it.
Carroll, R. T. divine fallacy (argument from incredulity). The Skeptic's Dictionary. Read in full; source for the alias and for the quoted form of the argument.
Argument from incredulity. Wikipedia. Source text read on 17 August 2026 for what the article cites and what it says.
